## Discussion

The main lesson of this study is methodological as much as empirical. The comparison between the iEEG atlas and source-reconstructed HD-EEG does not reduce to a single question of whether one dataset reproduces the other. The final result will depend from many assumptions (what counts as oscillatory power and how to best measure it) and different spectral techniques turn the same data into different comparison objects. Among many summaries of the neural activity at the spectrum ,  all summaries are closely related , but not all  are  interchangeable.

The two modalities  in question (iEEG and HD EEG) did not differ only in overall quality or strength of signal. 
Source-reconstructed HD-EEG produced a narrow, high-amplitude alpha-dominated pattern, whereas the iEEG atlas showed a broader distribution of peaks across alpha, beta, low gamma, and high gamma, together with a different aperiodic shape,
. Depending on the chosen  descriptor, this contrast can look like partial cross-modal recovery or failure, also already discussed  in literature change in the apparent oscillatory pattern after aperiodic correction. The result  or questions is therefore not one stable answer hidden behind several analyses, but a demonstration that the answer depends on how "oscillation," "frequency", and "agreement" are operationalised. This might be seeming familar and obvious caveat known for many scientistist that the operarationalisation matter in how we answer to our questions, yet this variety of terminologies and might hamper/slow our undersrandaing and  clinical progres by giving heteregenity of answett?

The alpha pattern is the most robust point of convergence across descriptors, but the interpretation of beta and gamma activity changes across relative power, fitted peaks, and subtraction residuals. The aperiodic exponent is not a fixed property waiting to be read from the spectrum either: in iEEG it depends strongly on whether the spectrum is treated as fixed or knee-shaped, while in source HD-EEG it is more stable across methods. The chapter therefore uses the cross-modal comparison not only to ask what HD-EEG can recover from iEEG, but also to show which spectral conclusions are robust to the analytical route used to obtain them.

### Branching Paths

This chapter set out as a narrower comparison and widened as the surrounding methodological literature did. Several of the studies that now anchor the analysis were published after the project began, and the scope had to be closed at some point rather than tracked indefinitely. The analysis has the structure of a garden of forking paths [@gelman2013GardenForkingPaths]: many defensible operational choices were available before the results were interpreted, in how oscillations are extracted, how frequency is represented, and how cross-modal agreement is summarised. Rather than commit to one pipeline, we report several branches and ask which conclusions survive across them.

Two choices shaped the analysis enough to state directly. First, we avoided relative band power as a basis for inference. Relative powers are compositional: within each channel the bands are normalised to a fixed total, so they cannot vary independently and ordinary correlation across them is not valid [@filzmoser2012CorrelationAnalysisCompositional]. We kept the untransformed maps as a descriptive summary and carried inference with the aperiodic-separated peak descriptors instead. Second, summarising a multivariate, multi-region, multi-band comparison is itself a data-reduction problem, and much of the work is carried by visualisation: several figures present closely related information from different angles, because no single reduction captures the comparison without discarding something that matters elsewhere.

Different spectral methods rest on different assumptions about what in the power spectrum counts as the phenomenon, so they construct different versions of it rather than offering different windows onto one stable spectral truth.
Each descriptor makes a different "spectral object" available. These are operationalisations, and under methodological pluralism each can be partly
valid: each sets its own identity conditions for what is being compared. The models are constructed, but they are not arbitrary, and some are more useful
than others in a clinical context. The potential cost  is that referring loosely to "the" spectral measure, or moving between measures without saying which, breeds confusion and can yield contradictory claims about a biomarker's
validity. <!-- alidity here is an evidence-based constraint on the empirical setup and the measuring apparatus: imperfect, plural, and mediated by tools, but a constraint nonetheless.aparatus, even if imperfect plural and mediated by tools -->

### What is recovered, what is not

Alpha is the strongest cross-modal signal, and preservation is band-dependent. On uncorrected relative-power maps, regional agreement was clearest in alpha (r = 0.60) and weaker in delta (r = 0.42), with essentially none in theta (r = 0.13), only weak agreement in beta (r = 0.30), and an anti-correlation in gamma (r = −0.29). Modelling the oscillations explicitly and removing the aperiodic background did not shift this pattern: agreement of regional peak prevalence stayed confined to the low and mid bands (alpha ρ = 0.60, beta ρ = 0.47) against delta ρ = 0.04, theta ρ = −0.07 and gamma ρ = −0.25. But those results we should 

The descriptor used to detect peaks was itself unstable, and that instability is part of the finding. The k-means clustering solution, the no-peak reference set, and the data-driven interval definition all shifted with reasonable changes to preprocessing and fitting range, and the 4% power rule of the original atlas did not transfer to the source-reconstructed spectra: applied to HD-EEG it over-segmented the high-frequency tail, a consequence of the unit-power normalisation rather than of physiological structure. Because the clustering descriptor was not robust to these choices, we did not carry it forward to the aperiodic-corrected spectra, and characterised oscillatory content with the more stable per-band parametrised-peak descriptor, which needs neither a clustering step nor a no-peak reference. The instability is not noise around a true answer; it is a reason to prefer one operationalisation over another.


That alpha specifically is recovered fits its tie to laminar and feedback/feedforward circuit architecture [@jensen2026AlphaRhythmPhysiology], which suggests the recovered structure reflects broader circuit organisation rather than isolated narrowband generators. It sits between two adjacent literatures: @janiukstyte2023NormativeBrainMapping found comparable scalp-EEG gradients but without joint aperiodic treatment, and Afnan et al. [-@afnan2023ValidatingMEGSource] found partial MEG recovery with lateral regions recovered better than deep or medial ones. This chapter adds a non-invasive modality more vulnerable to source mixing than MEG, and treats periodic and aperiodic features together.


### Methodological dependencies of aperiodic estimates

The aperiodic exponent reported for iEEG is a modelling choice as much as a property of the spectrum. The knee and fixed models returned very different iEEG exponents (median $\chi$ = 3.30 vs 1.94) that correlated only moderately across channels (r = 0.49), because forcing a single line through a spectrum with a genuine knee biases the exponent low by a channel-specific amount. In source HD-EEG, where the knee is essentially absent, the two exponents nearly coincided (0.94 vs 0.93; r = 0.88). The fitting range mattered the same asymmetric way: narrowing the fixed-mode range from 1-80 Hz to 1-45 Hz lowered the iEEG exponent by a near-constant offset (mean Δχ ≈ +0.47, broadly distributed across regions), while leaving the HD-EEG exponent essentially unchanged ($\Delta\chi$≈ −0.04). Cross-modal exponent comparisons must therefore hold the fitting range fixed, and are only interpretable below ~45 Hz, where the two modalities behave comparably.

Two checks bound how far these dependencies are artefacts of the parameterisation. In HD-EEG the specparam fixed-mode exponent and the IRASA fractal exponent agreed almost perfectly over the same band (r = 0.97), so the recovered slope is aligning with results obtained via other methods in the source data: the cross-modal and range effects are properties of the spectra, not of specparam. The remaining dependency is the functional form itself, since the same data fit with a 1/f versus a knee (Lorentzian-shaped) aperiodic model yield different exponents whenever a knee is present. This sits alongside reports that the exponent depends on the estimation range [@boncompte2026AperiodicExponentBrain; @gerster2022SeparatingNeuralOscillations; @wilson2024ModelSelectionSpectral], and alongside Ameen et al. [-@ameen2025TemporallyResolvedAnalyses], who, working on this same iEEG-plus-HD-EEG dataset in sleep, found that whether the knee is included substantially affects stage-dependent variation. Our wakefulness result, that iEEG needs the knee and HD-EEG does not, is consistent with theirs and reinforces selecting the aperiodic mode per modality rather than imposing one form across both.

### Methodological caveats and limitations

The limitations fall into three groups: data-level constraints on the comparison itself, methodological dependencies of the parameterisation, and limits on what convergence across metrics can establish.

**Data-level.** No simultaneously recorded iEEG-and-scalp dataset was available, so the comparison is between two cohorts recorded under different conditions, and modality cannot be cleanly separated from condition or population. The Frauscher iEEG atlas was recorded with eyes closed, the HD-EEG dataset with eyes open. Eye state affects oscillatory activity, most strongly posterior alpha power, and may also affect the aperiodic exponent and offset @geller2014EyeClosureCauses. <!-- FLAG: this is the only plain-text citation in the chapter; the rest use @keys. Add the BibTeX key (e.g. @geller2014...) for consistency. --> Where cross-modal agreement is observed, it is observed despite this difference in condition; where it is weak, modality and condition cannot be separated with these data. The aggregation structures also differ: 1772 channels across 106 patients in iEEG against 1444 virtual sensors across 19 subjects in HD-EEG, so per-region statistics are pooled differently, which should be kept in mind when interpreting between-region differences. Finally, the atlas was recorded in patients with refractory epilepsy; only channels in non-epileptogenic regions were retained, but how far these spectral features generalise to non-epileptic populations is a known limitation of the reference [@frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial].

**Method-level.** Spectral parameterisation depends on the assumed aperiodic form, the fitting range, and the peak-detection thresholds; the chapter addresses this dependency directly in the stability analyses above, but the estimates should still be read as conditional on those choices [@donoghue2021MethodologicalConsiderationsStudying]. The paremetrisation was introduced by the promise of data driven infrernce avoiding arbitrary choices, but the complexity is still present. A subset of source-reconstructed spectra showed near-flat slopes with exponents near zero, low fit quality (R² < 0.70), no clear 1/f structure, and peaks confined to beta where present. These are unlikely to reflect genuine neural dynamics with an unusually flat broadband component; more plausibly they come from source labels that receive little coherent signal after inverse modelling, so the reconstructed time course is dominated by spatially smoothed noise or leakage from neighbouring regions [@tait2021SystematicEvaluationSource]. Biophysical modelling suggests high-frequency broadband power in scalp EEG may not be neural in origin [@brake2025ContributionsActionPotentials; @brake2024NeurophysiologicalBasisAperiodic], and this carries over to source-reconstructed data, where the inverse solution cannot recover signal absent at the sensor level. Fitting the fixed aperiodic model to such spectra yields nominally valid parameters that should not be read as cortical broadband dynamics [@wilson2024ModelSelectionSpectral; @gerster2022SeparatingNeuralOscillations]. <!-- Sources with R² below 0.90 were flagged and the sensitivity of regional results to their inclusion or exclusion was assessed. --> <!-- TODO: state the outcome of this sensitivity check — the Results report the flagging (99.7% iEEG vs 74.0% HD passed R²>0.9) but I could not find the inclusion/exclusion result stated, so I did not write one in. --> A further confound here is waveform shape: non-sinusoidal rhythms generate harmonics that specparam can fit as separate peaks, which can inflate apparent high-band peak counts in either modality.

That is the contribution: a non-invasive validation against intracranial EEG using HD-EEG rather than MEG [@afnan2023ValidatingMEGSource], treating periodic and aperiodic features together rather than band power alone [@janiukstyte2023NormativeBrainMapping], and read across several agreement metrics rather than one. It does not show that normative HD-EEG maps are ready for clinical use, that these patterns hold across populations or recording conditions, or that source HD-EEG can stand in for iEEG at fine spatial scale. What it offers is a map of which regional spectral measures survive the move to a non-invasive modality, and under which modelling choices: the groundwork others would build a biomarker or mapping study on, not the study itself.

### Further steps

Two extensions follow directly from the present design, beyond the controlled-simulation evaluation of cross-modal metrics noted above. A simultaneously recorded iEEG-and-scalp dataset would let modality, recording condition, and population be separated, which the present two-cohort comparison cannot do. And the same joint periodic/aperiodic comparison could be run between reconstructed sources and other modalities at the sensor level, and across different parcellation atlases, to test how far the recoverable structure depends on the specific atlas and source model used.
